messages.subject: How to analyse clustered randomised experiments? (increased Type-I error in lme4?)
messages.subject_clean: How to analyse clustered randomised experiments? (increased Type-I error in lme4?)
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I'm trying to figure out the effect of randomising the assignment of 
treatments to groups of subjects (e.g. classes) rather than on the level 
of subjects. In rather a lot of studies in applied linguistics, 
treatments (e.g. pedagogical interventions) are administered at the 
school or class levels but the grouping variable isn't always taken into 
account in the analyses. I therefore ran a couple of simulations to see 
how this would affect the results.

To investigate the effect of ignoring clustering in the analyses, I 
analysed data of a simulated clustered randomised experiment using 
ordinary ANOVAs and using lme4 with a by-group random intercept (details 
below). The Type-I error rate of the ANOVAs was much larger than the 
nominal rate. But the lme4-based results were also skewed towards 
anti-conservative p values. Am I missing something?

I should add that I haven't fully immersed myself in the literature on 
clustered randomised experiments, so you're welcome to chasten me if so 
inclined.

Cheers,
Jan

###

SIMULATIONS

The basic set-up of one run of simulations was as follows. 10 classes 
with 20 pupils each participated in a pedagogical intervention (to 
improve their L2 lexical skills or whatever). The 10 classes were 
randomly assigned to either the control or the experimental condition in 
a post-test-only design. The classes were left intact, i.e. all pupils 
in a given class were assigned to the same condition.

The post-test scores were constructed as follows:

score = overall_mean + intervention_effect + effect_cluster + error

For these simulations, effect_cluster was normally distributed with M = 
0 and SD = 1 ('sdClasses'), whereas the SD of the error term was 3 
('sdParts'). In other words, the intra-class correlation coefficient was 
1^2/(1^2 + 3^2) = 0.10. As a first step, I took a look at Type-I errors 
and therefore set the Treatment effect to 0.

The following functions (were supposed to :)) create datasets 
(createData.fnc()), analyse the simulated data using normal ANOVAs and a 
hierarchical model with 'Class' as the grouping factor and return the 
respective p values (analyseLMER.fnc()). simulate.fnc() combines both 
functions, which are then passed on to replicate().

#################

createData.fnc <- function(nrClasses = 10, # even number below 26
                            nrPartsPerClass = 20, # even number
                            sdClasses = 1,
                            sdParts = 3,
                            Treatment = 0) {

   Classes <- data.frame(Class = letters[1:nrClasses],
                         EffectClass = rnorm(nrClasses, 0, sdClasses), # 
by-class adjustment
                         GroupClass = c(rep("control", nrClasses/2), # 
assign control classes
                                        rep("intervention", 
nrClasses/2)) # and intervention classes
   )

   Data <- data.frame(Class = rep(letters[1:nrClasses], nrPartsPerClass),
                      EffectParts = rnorm(nrClasses * nrPartsPerClass, 
0, sdParts) # by-participant error
   )

   Data <- merge(Data, Classes, by="Class")

   Data$Score = Data$EffectParts + Data$EffectClass + 
(as.numeric(Data$GroupClass)-1)*Treatment

   return(Data)
}

analyseLMER.fnc <- function(Data = Data) {
   pNoCluster = anova(lm(Score ~ GroupClass, Data))$'Pr(>F)'[1]
   pCluster = anova(lmer(Score ~ (1|Class), Data, REML=FALSE),
                                lmer(Score ~ GroupClass + (1|Class), 
Data, REML = FALSE))$'Pr(>Chisq)'[2]
   return(list(pNoCluster, pCluster))
}

simulate.fnc <- function(nrClasses = 10, nrPartsPerClass = 20, sdClasses 
= 1, sdParts = 3, Treatment = 0) {
   Data <- createData.fnc(nrClasses = nrClasses, nrPartsPerClass = 
nrPartsPerClass, sdClasses = sdClasses, sdParts = sdParts, Treatment = 
Treatment)
   pVals <- analyseLMER.fnc(Data = Data)
   return(pVals)
}

library(lme4)

pVals <- replicate(5000, simulate.fnc())

#################

hist(unlist(pVals[1,]), main="No grouping variable", xlab="pval")
table(unlist(pVals[1,]) < 0.05)

##FALSE  TRUE
## 3788  1212 # i.e. 5-fold increase in Type I error


hist(unlist(pVals[2,]), main="Grouping variable", xlab="pval")
table(unlist(pVals[2,]) < 0.05)

##FALSE  TRUE
  ##4599   401 # better, but still appreciably more than 5%

##############

messages.body_plain:
I've been doing some research on this issue (i.e., I've been running 
some more simulations). One approach seems to be to take the t-value of 
the intervention effect and relate this to a t-distribution with 
nrClasses - 2 degrees of freedom. As you'd expect, this yields much 
p-values that are much too low: in 1,000 simulation runs under the null, 
I got merely 16 significant results.

A more accurate alternative is to use parametric bootstrapping, e.g.:

###

fit <- lmer(Score ~ GroupClass + (1|Class), Data)
nullfit <- lmer(Score ~ (1|Class), Data)

tvals <- replicate(1000, {
   Data$Sim <- unlist(simulate(nullfit))
   bsFit <- lmer(Sim ~ GroupClass + (1|Class), Data)
   t <- coef(summary(bsFit))["GroupClassintervention", "t value"]
   return(t)
}

t.fit <- coef(summary(fit))["GroupClassintervention", "t value"]
pParBS <- 1 - table(abs(tvals) >= abs(t.fit))[1] / 1000

###

It's a bit cumbersome to run a lot of simulations with a parametric 
bootstrap in them, but one run was right on the mark with 50 significant 
results out of 1000.
